beats.say: Here's the real secret. When Costco gets bigger and buys cheaper, it doesn't keep the savings. It cuts prices. Lower prices bring more shoppers. More shoppers mean bigger volumes. Bigger volumes mean cheaper buying. And round again. Even the shoppers at the oldest stores benefit, every time a new one opens.

beats.say: And he spotted the paradox at its heart. The company grows by giving more back. Ask most companies what they'd do with windfall profits, and they'll spend it, or return it to shareholders. Almost no one replies, give it back to customers. That, he wrote, is why competing with Costco is so hard.

beats.say: Now the defence. One. Thin margins leave very little room for mistakes. Two. The contract lives only as long as management resists temptation. One greedy boss, and it's gone. Three. Sleep himself warned that a low share price could invite a buyout at a bad price. And four. This kind of culture is very hard to build later. It usually has to be there from day one.

beats.say: One. When its costs fall, do its prices fall too? Two. Roughly how much does a customer save, for every rupee the company keeps? Three. If it had a windfall, would management give some back to customers?
